analysis.one_liner: Caps imports of nonrubber footwear to protect domestic shoe factories and their workers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the House Ways and Means Committee's trade subcommittee until the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Commerce Secretary to estimate U.S. shoe consumption each year and cap imports of nonrubber footwear at a rising share of it — 60 percent of consumption in the first two years, climbing to 69 percent by year five — and to divide that cap among foreign countries. Its stated goal was to stop the decline of the domestic shoe industry, which had lost 147,300 jobs and seen the import share of the U.S. market climb from 51 percent in 1981 to 83 percent in 1988. A quota like this protects factory jobs in shoe towns, but it does so by making every pair of shoes more expensive for American consumers.
analysis.who_benefits: Domestic nonrubber footwear makers and their workers, concentrated in small manufacturing towns, would gain a guaranteed share of the U.S. market. The bill's own findings describe plants closing in small towns that depend on shoe factories, and it would have cut the imported share of the market back toward 60 percent.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Domestic shoe factories and their workers

how_it_helps.text: Caps footwear imports at 60 percent of estimated domestic consumption in the first two years, rising to 63, 66, and 69 percent in later years, reserving a larger share of the U.S. market for domestic producers.
The bill's findings state the industry lost 147,300 footwear jobs and 1,053 plants since 1968, and that imported footwear rose from 51 percent of the U.S. market in 1981 to 83 percent in 1988.

Directs the Commerce Secretary to allocate the import limits among foreign countries based on past import levels, unfair trade findings, and market trends, and to enforce the cap through an import licensing system.

analysis.who_pays: Shoe buyers. An import cap tightens supply of a product that made up 83 percent of the market, so consumers would pay more for footwear across the board, and the cost falls hardest on lower-income households. Importers and retailers also lose sales.
analysis.who_pays_short: American shoe buyers and footwear importers

drawbacks.text: A quota raises shoe prices for every American consumer to protect one industry; the benefit goes to a specific group of producers and workers while the cost is spread across tens of millions of shoe purchases each year.

The cap would remain even as the domestic industry's cost disadvantage persisted, locking in protection for five years rather than addressing why foreign shoes cost less, and foreign countries could retaliate against other U.S. exports.
Importers would face a new federal licensing system and fees just to bring shoes into the country, adding administrative cost on top of the quota itself.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered real help to a specific group — shoe factory workers in towns with few other employers — and its authors pointed to three International Trade Commission findings of serious injury. But the mechanism was a quota that raises prices on a common consumer good for everyone, and the cost per job preserved, spread across all shoe buyers, would have been far larger than the wages saved. It protected an existing industry rather than helping displaced workers adjust, which is why proposals like this routinely drew opposition from economists, retailers, and importers.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee and then to its trade subcommittee, which never acted on it, so the bill died quietly when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. William Goodling introduced the bill on January 24, 1989, the same day it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
Three days later, on January 27, 1989, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Trade, the usual first step for trade bills.
No further action appears in the record — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the bill died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.
The bill had only six cosponsors — three Republicans and three Democrats — far short of what it would have taken to move a quota bill through committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Footwear importers, foreign shoe manufacturers, and American shoe buyers came out ahead, since they kept the lower prices and wider selection that an import quota would have taken away. The domestic shoe industry got nothing and continued to shrink.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Shoe importers, foreign makers, and consumers

for.name: Rep. William F. Goodling
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cap nonrubber footwear imports at a share of domestic consumption, citing 147,300 lost industry jobs since 1968.

for.name: Rep. Benjamin Gilman
for.what_they_did: Joined Goodling in introducing the bill on the day it was filed.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Dan Rostenkowski (D-MA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and never reported it out; no hearing or markup appears in the record.

against.name: Subcommittee on Trade of House Ways and Means
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on January 27, 1989 and took no recorded action for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Bush administration
against.what_they_did: Opposed new mandatory import quotas on footwear, making enactment of a quota bill of this kind unlikely without a veto-level fight.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was evenly bipartisan — three Republicans and three Democrats — but with only six cosponsors and no recorded votes, the bill never got far enough for a partisan split to show.

industries.note: The quota would have guaranteed them roughly 31 to 40 percent of the U.S. shoe market, rescuing an industry losing share to imports. Their gain comes directly out of consumers' pockets, since the cap makes every pair of shoes more expensive.

industries.industry: Footwear importers and foreign shoe producers
industries.note: A hard cap on entry, allocated by country and enforced through licenses and fees, would sharply reduce the volume they could sell and raise their costs. Their interest in defeating it ran alongside consumers' interest in cheaper shoes.
Retailers would face a smaller, pricier, less varied supply of footwear and a new import-permit burden on their suppliers. Cheaper imports kept their costs down and their shelves full.

industries.industry: U.S. shoe factory towns and supplier businesses
industries.note: The bill's findings emphasize that shoe plants are the economic anchor of small towns and that plant closings threaten the industry's supplier base. Workers in these towns would have been the direct human beneficiaries of the quota.
